facts.fact_text: Hyde Park continued staging protests and demonstrations after being struck off the Government's list of non-governmental organisations.
On 30 August 2007, at 7.30 a.m., the applicants started their protest in front of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.
At 9 a.m. on 4 September 2007, the applicants started their protest in front of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.
In the morning of 10 September 2007, several members of Hyde Park started to protest in front of the buildings of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Prosecutor General's Office.
Immediately after the applicants started their protest on 30 August 2007, a police officer approached them and ordered them to stop the protest.

The police officer ordered the applicants to stop the protest because the Municipal Council of Chișinău's authorisation of 20 August 2007 had been challenged by the Prosecutor General's Office in court on 29 August 2007.
The applicants refused to comply with the police officer's order to stop the protest on 30 August 2007.
Mr Ghenadie Brega was arrested on 30 August 2007 and taken to a police station where he was questioned.
Mr Oleg Brega was arrested on 30 August 2007 and taken to a police station where he was questioned.
Mr Hristea-Stan was arrested on 30 August 2007 and taken to a police station where he was questioned.
Mr Juraveli was arrested on 30 August 2007 and taken to a police station where he was questioned.
At approximately 9.30 a.m. on 30 August 2007, Mr Ghenadie Brega, Mr Oleg Brega, Mr Hristea-Stan and Mr Juraveli were released without explanation.
At 9.25 a.m. on 4 September 2007, Mr Ghenadie Brega was arrested on the ground that the demonstration had not been authorised.
At 9.25 a.m. on 4 September 2007, Mr Oleg Brega was arrested on the ground that the demonstration had not been authorised.
At 9.25 a.m. on 4 September 2007, a Hyde Park member who is not an applicant in the present case was arrested on the ground that the demonstration had not been authorised.
Mr Ghenadie Brega, Mr Oleg Brega and the non-applicant Hyde Park member were taken to a police station on 4 September 2007 where they were body searched.
Mr Ghenadie Brega, Mr Oleg Brega and the non-applicant Hyde Park member were kept at the police station for approximately five hours on 4 September 2007.

Several minutes after the Hyde Park members began protesting on 10 September 2007, the police arrived and arrested Mr Juraveli on the ground that the authorisation did not contain the names of all the persons involved in the protest.

Several minutes after the Hyde Park members began protesting on 10 September 2007, the police arrived and arrested Mr Oleg Brega on the ground that the authorisation did not contain the names of all the persons involved in the protest.

Several minutes after the Hyde Park members began protesting on 10 September 2007, the police arrived and arrested Mr Hristea-Stan on the ground that the authorisation did not contain the names of all the persons involved in the protest.
The authorisation required the protest to be held at a distance of at least fifty metres from the buildings of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Prosecutor General's Office.
Section 11(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that not later than fifteen days prior to the date of the assembly, the organiser shall submit a notification to the Municipal Council.

Section 11(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate the name of the organiser and the aim of the assembly, the date, starting time and finishing time, the location and access and return routes, the manner in which the assembly is to take place, the approximate number of participants, the persons responsible for the sound conduct of the assembly, and the services the organiser asks the Municipal Council to provide.

Section 12(6) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the local authorities can reject an application to hold an assembly only if, after having consulted the police, it has obtained convincing evidence that the provisions of sections 6 and 7 of the Assemblies Act will be breached with serious consequences for society.

Section 14(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that a decision rejecting the application for holding an assembly shall be reasoned and presented in writing, and shall contain reasons for refusing to issue the authorisation.
Section 15(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the organiser of the assembly can challenge the refusal in the administrative courts.
The police officer argued that according to the Law on the Prosecutor's Office, the prosecutor's appeal against an administrative act suspended the latter's action until after a court examined it.

The Government maintained that Mr Juraveli, Mr Oleg Brega and Mr Hristea-Stan had been detained on 10 September 2007 for breach of the peace and for having shouted insults about the Minister for Internal Affairs.

The head of the police station of the Centru District dismissed the criminal complaint on the ground that the Municipal Council of Chișinău's authorisation of 20 August 2007 contained numerous flaws, including a failure to indicate the exact place of the protest.

The head of the police station of the Centru District dismissed the criminal complaint on the ground that the Municipal Council of Chișinău's authorisation of 20 August 2007 failed to indicate the number of participants.
The Prosecutor General's Office's appeal against the Municipal Council of Chișinău's authorisation of 20 August 2007 appears never to have been examined by the courts.
The Centru District Court dismissed the applicants' submissions regarding the demonstration of 4 September 2007.

The Centru District Court found that the applicants had breached section 11(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 by failing to submit the application within fifteen days in advance of the planned assembly.
According to the Centru District Court, the protest should have been held on 14 September 2007 at the earliest.

Article 32(1) of the Constitution of the Republic of Moldova guarantees each citizen freedom of thought, of opinion, and freedom of expression in public through words, images or through other available means.
Article 32(2) of the Constitution of the Republic of Moldova provides that freedom of expression shall not harm the honour or dignity of others or the right of others to have their own opinion.

Article 32(3) of the Constitution of the Republic of Moldova provides that the law prohibits and punishes the contestation and defamation of the State and the nation, calls to war and aggression, national, racial or religious hatred, incitement to discrimination, territorial separatism, or public violence, as well as other expression which endangers the constitutional order.

Article 40 of the Constitution of the Republic of Moldova provides that all meetings, demonstrations, rallies, processions or any other assemblies are free, and they may be organised and take place only peacefully and without the use of weapons.

Section 6(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall be conducted peacefully, without any sort of weapons, and shall ensure the protection of participants and the environment, without impeding the normal use of public highways, road traffic and the operation of economic undertakings and without degenerating into acts of violence capable of endangering the public order and the physical integrity and life of persons or their property.

Section 7 of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies shall be suspended in circumstances including denial and defamation of the State and of the people, incitement to war or aggression, incitement to hatred on ethnic, racial or religious grounds, incitement to discrimination, territorial separatism or public violence, and acts that undermine the constitutional order.

Section 8(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that assemblies may be conducted in squares, streets, parks and other public places in cities, towns and villages, and also in public buildings.

Section 8(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct an assembly in the buildings of the public authorities, the local authorities, prosecutors' offices, the courts or companies with armed security.

Section 8(3)(a) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct assemblies within fifty metres of the parliament building, the residence of the President of Moldova, the seat of the government, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court of Justice.

Section 8(3)(b) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that it shall be forbidden to conduct assemblies within twenty-five metres of the buildings of the central administrative authority, the local public authorities, courts, prosecutors' offices, police stations, prisons and social rehabilitation institutions, military installations, railway stations, airports, hospitals, companies which use dangerous equipment and machines, and diplomatic institutions.
Section 8(4) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that free access to the premises of the institutions listed in section 8(3) shall be guaranteed.
Section 8(5) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the local public authorities may, if the organisers agree, establish places or buildings for permanent assemblies.
Section 11(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that not later than fifteen days prior to the date of the assembly, the organiser shall submit a notification to the Municipal Council.

Section 11(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall indicate the name of the organiser and the aim of the assembly, the date, starting time and finishing time, the location and access and return routes, the manner in which the assembly is to take place, the approximate number of participants, the persons responsible for the sound conduct of the assembly, and the services the organiser asks the Municipal Council to provide.

Section 11(3) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that if the situation so requires, the Municipal Council may alter certain aspects of the prior notification with the agreement of the organiser of the assembly.

Section 12(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the prior notification shall be examined by the local government of the town or village at the latest five days before the date of the assembly.

Section 12(2) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that when the prior notification is considered at an ordinary or extraordinary meeting of the Municipal Council, the discussion shall deal with the form, timetable, location and other conditions for the conduct of the assembly and the decision taken shall take account of the specific situation.

Section 12(6) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the local authorities can reject an application to hold an assembly only if, after having consulted the police, it has obtained convincing evidence that the provisions of sections 6 and 7 of the Assemblies Act will be breached with serious consequences for society.

Section 14(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that a decision rejecting the application for holding an assembly shall be reasoned and presented in writing, and shall contain reasons for refusing to issue the authorisation.
Section 15(1) of the Assemblies Act of 21 June 1995 provides that the organiser of the assembly can challenge the refusal in the administrative courts.
